speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF MEETING ON SATELLITE COMMUNICATIONS SYSTEM
speechtext:
I wish to inform the house that Canada has accepted an invitation from the British government to participate in a commonwealth conference in London from March 28 to April 13, to discuss the role of the commonwealth in the development of world wide communications systems based on satellites. The Canadian government has followed with keen interest the research which has been taking place in this field in recent years, mainly in the United States. We are very interested in exploring with other countries, including of course the United States, the
basis of future co-operation among the countries of the world in developing communications based on earth satellites.

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF MEETING ON SATELLITE COMMUNICATIONS SYSTEM
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should just like to comment on that announcement, if I may, and say that I think the Prime Minister is well advised in doing what he has announced. There have been from time to time, originating in the Department of Transport, I believe, telecommunications conferences and the like which the Prime Minister has in mind, but this one of course has a much broader and wider view and I think the house will welcome the announcement made by the Prime Minister.

Last night, Mr. Chairman, you gave me the floor about ten minutes before the committee was due to rise, and about half of that time was occupied by interruptions, mainly from the Minister of Public
Supply-Public Works
Works. My colleague the hon. member for Levis attempted to raise a point of order about this, but since you ruled that there was no point of order perhaps you will permit me to deal with this matter as a question of privilege.
When the minister intervened I was dealing with the government's housing policy. I had endeavoured to make the point that the fact the government finds it necessary to go so heavily into the housing business is an indication that there is something wrong with the government's fiscal and monetary policy which failed to produce the economic climate in which private enterprise, whose normal function it is to provide for the needs of the people, was able to operate in the housing field.
At that point the minister rose to interrupt. I thought he was going to correct an error I had made, because I recognize that we all make slips of the tongue especially when we are attempting to think on our feet. But the minister did not do that. What the minister proceeded to do was to debate my comment. In his rebuttal the minister did not deal with the point I was making with respect to housing policy. He proceeded to deal with public works, and made statements as to how much this government had spent on public works in my province. I intend to deal with that statement later.
My question of privilege is this. If the procedure is adopted by the house of allowing a minister or anyone else to interrupt at any time the member who has the floor in order to start debating subjects which are not under discussion, bedlam will result. The minister has no more right to interrupt than any other person.
Your Honour made the point that I conceded the floor to the minister. I did so because I thought he was going to correct a statement I had made, but the minister took advantage of that opportunity. We do not know what the minister is going to say when he rises. We have to trust to his sense of fairness and proportion in matters like this. When he does not observe the ordinary rules of procedure he is out of order. I do not mind conceding the floor if the minister requests that I do so and states for what purpose he is rising, but I shall not yield just to permit a red herring to be brought into the argument I am advancing.
Since the minister has undertaken to intervene in my remarks I would ask Your Honour to count my time as from now and not as from five minutes to ten o'clock, as would normally be the case.
As I said, a national housing policy should operate in such a way as to treat all parts of the nation alike as far as humanly

Supply-Public Works
possible. The figures the minister produced yesterday illustrate that the government's housing policy is creating an overexpansion in economic activity in one province and is doing little to correct the underexpansion in other parts of the country. In my opinion a government policy should operate with the purpose of having quite the reverse effect. It should try to level out economic expansion and make it more uniform throughout the whole country.
I pointed out to the committee that unemployment is always a serious problem in the Atlantic provinces, and during the winter months when it is at its peak it can reach and has reached in my province as high as 25 per cent of the labour force. The Minister of National Revenue seemed to ridicule that statement, and I want to put some figures on Hansard to support what I said. It is true that since 1960 we do not have a separate breakdown of percentages of unemployment in the various provinces; instead we have figures for the whole Atlantic region.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, on a point or order, I suggest that we are talking about public works, not unemployment, and I think we should at least keep on the subject.

I am going to relate the figures I am about to give to the housing policy of the government. I think what I have already said proves that there is a relationship between housing policy and employment, just as there is a relationship between the fiscal policy of the government and the extent to which it has to engage in the housing business.
I am sorry that the Minister of National Revenue is not here to listen to this, since he questioned my statement last night. In 1960, the last year for which we had a percentage breakdown by provinces, unemployment in the Atlantic provinces was 14.4 per cent of the work force. That was in the winter months. I believe in January, and probably not at the worst period. At that particular time when the average for the Atlantic provinces was 14.4 per cent the average for the province of Newfoundland was 25 per cent, and the situation got worse.
The figures released by the bureau of statistics a short time ago give the percentages as of the 13th of January, which is not the peak so far as unemployment is concerned, and the percentage for the Atlantic provinces was 14.7 per cent. If there were 25 per cent unemployed in Newfoundland in 1960, when the average for the Atlantic provinces was 14.4 per cent, surely it is reasonable to assume that the figure was at least 25 per cent and perhaps worse for Newfoundland

when the average for the Atlantic provinces was 14.7 per cent as of January 13.
What percentage of that 25 per cent were fishermen?

Well, are fishermen not people?
Are they not workers?

My hon. friend knows that fishermen cannot draw unemployment insurance and fish at the same time. They cannot fish at certain periods because it is a seasonal occupation. My hon. friend knows that the figures are not in proportion to the facts.

I want to support my statement with some figures compiled by the Atlantic provinces economic council, and the source of their figures is the special surveys division of the dominion bureau of statistics. I ask the hon. member for St. John's East to listen to this, because I am now talking about averages for the whole year and not seasonal unemployment when the fishermen are included. In 1958 there were 20,000 unemployed Newfoundlanders out of a work force of 111,000. In 1959, according to the government's own publication, there were 22,000 Newfoundlanders out of work for the whole year out of a work force of 115,000.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I rise on a point of order, Mr. Chairman.
In 1960 there were 21,000 out of work out of a work force of 118,000.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I see the Solicitor General is rising on a point of order. I think I can anticipate what his point of order is. The statistics that are being placed on the record by the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo relate to unemployment, and they would be more appropriately discussed on the estimates of the Department of Labour. I do not want to be unfair or unduly restrictive to the hon. member, but I do feel that his suggestion that he would relate these figures to item 1 of the estimates of the Department of Public Works has not come through to me at this stage. I would ask him to move in that direction as soon as possible.

Would you let me say a
word on this point, Mr. Chairman? I submit that the minister should be ashamed of himself when he contends that these estimates for public works have no relationship whatever to unemployment. I think the minister should be ashamed of himself.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
I did not
say what the hon. member has just stated I said. When the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo is talking about unemployment he

should relate it to this Department of Public Works, and not give us a long harangue about it.

I wish to address myself to the point of order, Mr. Chairman, Your Honour will recall that the minister, in the opening statement he made yesterday on housing, in particular, mentioned that the consequence of government policy was that it had a direct effect on unemployment. If the minister was able to make that kind of argument I am sure that Your Honour, on reconsideration, will agree it is open to the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo to make a reply. That is all he has been doing.

I think the record will show that these figures are related to the housing policy of the government, and the government has gone into the housing question in a big way, as the minister pointed out, to prime the economic pump. Last night the minister made the statement that this government spent three times as much on public works in Newfoundland as did the Liberal government. If that is so that is as it should be, because-
Give us credit for it, then.

It is as it should be, because of the need to create employment in Newfoundland and also the need to even out the disparities in our economic development. If the housing policy of the government cannot achieve that, then certainly the public works program of this government should be operated in such a way as to make up for that lack. I am afraid that the minister's statements are not borne out by the facts.
We have raised the question of urban development in the northern section of St. John's for at least two years during the consideration of the estimates of this department. So far as I have been able to find out, that development has not taken place as yet. For a whole year the premier of Newfoundland was blamed for this situation. Over a year ago the premier went to the extent of making changes in the legislation so that the municipality of St. John's could cooperate with the federal government and leave the province out of the picture. However, this development is proceeding very slowly, and certainly there are no houses being built even though the project has been under consideration for at least two years and possibly longer.
If I may come back to the minister's statement about having spent three times as much in Newfoundland as his predecessors, I should like to take the figures for expenditures on public buildings in the years 1959-1960 to 1961-1962 inclusive. This government has
Supply-Public Works
spent $1.3 million on public buildings during that time, whereas their predecessors in the three years from 1954-1955 to 1957-1958, spent $8.5 million on public buildings, at a time when there was less disparity in the economic development of the various parts of our province. If we take the money spent on harbour development in the same period, we find that the total spent by this government according to the estimates, and I have only had time to go back three years, was $16.3 million as compared with $7.7 million under the Liberals. Now, that looks like a tremendous difference, but it is still not three times as great. If it were three times as great it would be $22 million. However, the figure of $16.3 million does not give the correct picture, because of that $16.3 million at least $9 million has been spent on the harbour of St. John's.
What is wrong with that?

There is nothing wrong with that; I should like to see more spent on improving the harbour of St. John's. However, there is this to be said about it. This $9 million that is being spent on the harbour of St. John's is not going into the pockets of Newfoundlanders. It is not increasing to any appreciable extent the purchasing power of the people of Newfoundland. This work is being done by a mainland contractor, and most of that money is going to benefit people on the mainland. I doubt if more than 20 per cent to 25 per cent of it is going into the pockets of the people of my province to increase their purchasing power.
If we take out this special amount for St John's, which as I said is not an important factor in the priming of our economic pump, then the average amount of money spent on public works per year by this government works out at a little under $3 million as compared with $4 million under the Liberal government from the years 1954-1955 to 1956-1957.

You were not shelved.

speechtext: You had better stick to Levis.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
I am hearing
several speakers at the same time, and I think we should allow the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo to speak for himself, which he can do very well as we all know.

Yesterday the minister mentioned the winter works program dealing with post offices, but there has not been very much money included in his estimates for that kind of work in my province. There was only $156,000 in 1960-61, $205,000 in 1961-62 and I think $180,000 for the coming fiscal year. That is a cause of complaint in my province, as we have certainly as great a

need as any other province. The minister did not make it clear whether this winter works program constituted a change in policy. We have been trying to get post offices built in many communities, but the projects have been turned down because the community revenues do not warrant them. I think we should change that policy and make our decisions not on the basis of revenue but on the basis of need of the number of people to be served, and particularly on the need to create employment in provinces which economically are lagging behind.
The work on St. John's harbour will soon be completed, and the minister tells us he is looking around for new projects. That being so I suggest to him that he give consideration to building a transshipment port in Newfoundland. There is a good site for such a port at Mortier bay. I believe it has been refered to in the MacPherson report on transportation, and I know the western grain shippers are interested in linking up shipping facilities at Mortier bay with the shipping facilities in Fort Churchill. This could be of great benefit both to Newfoundland and the western farmers in allowing them to ship their wheat more cheaply, and I would ask the minister to give consideration to the project.
I want to thank the minister for the increase this year in the harbours vote. It is $7.2 million as compared with $6.6 million last year, and when we make the deduction for the special project at St. John's harbour that works out to about $2.9 million for the rest of Newfoundland as compared with $1.8 million last year. There is only one disappointment in this so far as I am concerned, and that is that the minister has not seen fit to include anything in the estimates for the settlement of Seal Cove. I have requested this for the last four years, and in 1958 the minister's predecessor said he hoped something would be done within the following year. Correspondence which I had with his predecessor and himself went so far as to say that $90,000 would be listed for consideration in the 1960-61 estimates, but we are now dealing with the 1962-63 estimates and there is still no appropriation for this community.
There must be some misunderstanding about it, because this is a very urgent need. This little community of 600 or 700 people is completely isolated during the winter. If they need the services of a doctor or want to bring in food supplies their only communication is by sea, and they have no decent harbour whatsoever. Not only that, the economy of the community depends on the fishery, and without a harbour they cannot engage in fishing. When I was there last fall there was a provincial bulldozer in the place and,

through the co-operation of the district engineer at St. John's, I made arrangements to have the bulldozer scoop out the sand in the harbour. This meant that 30 fishermen were able to do some fishing whenever the weather permitted last fall, but that was too late in the year.
We had a debate on forestry a couple of days ago, and we were told the trend now is toward more mechanization in the woods. Therefore the alternative employment which this community has in the forests is going to disappear, and there will be less and less work for fewer people. This leaves them with the fishery. In any event, there are many people in that community who are now too old to go into the woods, and they must have some other form of livelihood apart from relief. This is an urgent matter, and I would not be raising it if I did not think it was urgent. I hope the minister will find time to consider it and include some appropriation in the supplementary estimates for this community.
There are just two other matters I want to refer to, and one of these is dredging. I am very glad to see that $594,000 has been appropriated for dredging in Newfoundland. That is a large item compared with other provinces, but it is still small in relation to the need because we have so many harbours that have not been dredged for 50 or 60 years.
The $560,000 for new equipment pleases me very much. I hope the minister will tell the committee when he replies just what equipment is going to be purchased with this sum. It does not seem large enough to buy the big, heavy suction dredge that is so badly needed. I have a situation in my riding, in the town of St. Lawrence, where they have been waiting now for five years for the harbour to be dredged out. This work has been postponed year after year in the hope that we can obtain the services of the suction dredge employed in Nova Scotia, but so far we have not been successful. In the meantime this situation is getting worse and worse with every passing week. Therefore there is a great need for a heavy suction dredge to be assigned to Newfoundland, which with Labrador has a tremendous coast line; we have 1,300 coastal harbours to be serviced.
In addition to this need for heavy dredging equipment, we have a need for shallow dredging equipment. I have urged this year after year, but the government seems to prefer to have this work done by private dredging firms. However, the fact is that there are not enough of these firms to do the work that requires to be done. This is not expensive equipment. We have so many small harbours where ordinary dredges cannot enter and operate, and perhaps there is a greater need
Supply-Public Works
for this type of equipment in Newfoundland than elsewhere. I ask the minister to keep this in mind.
The only other comment I wish to make is in connection with the miscellaneous vote. I was very happy when I looked at it and saw the amount to be voted was $2.4 million, but when I looked more closely I discovered that only $1,250,000 of this amount was going to be allocated for harbour improvement. That really is not enough in view of the drain on this vote which will be caused by projects that will cost up to $15,000 without treasury approval and can go as high as $25,000 with treasury approval. The amount is only $1,125,000 for the whole of Canada. Newfoundland's share of that is not going to be very much, and it will certainly all be used up on about a dozen projects costing $15,000 to $25,000. We are now reaching the point when we have a greater need for these small works, so I do hope the minister will give prompt consideration to increasing the amount of this vote.
In conclusion, Mr. Chairman, I wish to thank the committee for listening to me so patiently, and once more I would pay tribute to the minister and his staff in Ottawa for the co-operation they have extended in the past. I hope the same degree of co-operation will be forthcoming with respect to the few items that I have drawn to the attention of the minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, in answer to my hon. friend's question about the miscellaneous vote of $1,125,000 for Canada, of this amount more than one third is being spent in Newfoundland; the actual amount is $376,000. Is that enough?

I am not complaining on behalf of Newfoundland; what I am saying is that the vote for the whole of Canada is not enough. The $376,000 represents only a small share for Newfoundland if you divide that amount among the seven ridings, because you only have $50,000 per riding; and with a project cost of $15,000 to $25,000 you can only finance three or four works in each riding, whereas there are perhaps 30 or 40 projects which need to be taken care of and can only be taken care of out of this vote.
Mr. Her ridge: Mr. Chairman, first of all I wish to thank the minister for his courteous attention to any problem related to my constituency which I have brought to his notice. I must say that he has given every case careful consideration, whether the result has been positive or negative. I extend the same appreciation to the deputy minister, the senior officials in Ottawa, the district officials and the local officials of his department.

Supply-Public Works
As I have said before, this is a rather unusual department as far as I am concerned. I can say this because I have lived in very close relationship with the public works of Canada for over 56 years. When you live in the wilderness you do depend on them to put in a few dolphins or something of that nature to prevent you being shipwrecked, and so on.
I have inquired around over the years and have noticed there has been a steady improvement in the administration of this department since the reorganization into divisions some years ago. I was distinctly under the impression prior to the 1950's that the department was, in the first place, carrying too heavy a load for the staff and organization, and was trying to carry on in ways that were only suitable for a much smaller amount of work and responsibility. I think there has been a steady improvement in the administration. One division which has improved a great deal has been the property division and the placing of responsibility upon certain people's shoulders for the administration of buildings, and so on.
However, I have a few suggestions. I make them not in a critical spirit, but I place them before the minister in a co-operative mood, shall I say. I notice that the minister, the deputy minister and some of the senior officials of the department have visited the larger centres in Canada. I can only speak from my experience in British Columbia, but they have visited only the district offices in the main. I go into the district office, which is in Vancouver-I have known some of those chaps for a good many years-and I find that the minister and deputy minister have been to Vancouver and possibly up the coast in connection with reviewing the work of the branch. I might mention that I have a complaint in this regard. The British Columbia district office is known as the Vancouver district office. That is far too limited a connotation; it should be known as the British Columbia region of the Department of Public Works of Canada.
I do suggest that the minister, the deputy minister and the senior officials, particularly under the present circumstances, should stray rather further afield. They should personally and more frequently visit some of these districts where problems are developing. I have particular reference to, say, the Arrow lakes region. I am sure the minister has heard of the treaty known as the Columbia river treaty. If unfortunately the provisions of that treaty were carried out as they are written at the present time it would have a most unfortunate impact upon the property of the public works of Canada for a distance of 145 miles on the Arrow lakes. It would mean the destruction of 20 docks and innumerable

dolphins and other facilities which, if that situation did develop, would have to be replaced.
I think the problem is of such magnitude that the senior officials of this department should be giving it consideration so they may have the answers. I am quite sure that at the present time there is no firm estimate on the part of the Department of Public Works as to what it would cost to replace these facilities. And do not forget this; these would be replaced at ten times the cost of the present docks and wharfs and landing facilities because of the great variation of water levels and the longer docks that would be required.
I should like to bring another matter to the attention of the minister. This department has been spending money on the upper Duncan river for 20 years, but a senior official has never visited the Duncan river to study the problem there for himself. I do not think it is fair to local officials that these decisions should be left entirely to them. It is a heavy responsibility at times. It is the same on the lower Duncan. There has been some $5,000 a year spent there for years, and to good effect, but there are problems arising with respect to other developments in that area and I suggest the situation is one which should be considered by the deputy minister and the senior engineers.
To illustrate this, I would refer to the Trail river wall situation. The people of the district appreciate very much the government grant of 37$ per cent of the cost of the reconstruction of the Trail river wall. But this is an important project, a project of such a type in relation to other developments on the river that I think the deputy minister or senior officials should pay very close attention to it and not leave the responsibilty entirely to one engineer. There are serious problems with respect to foundations and so on which were not anticipated in the first estimate, and others will develop as time goes on.
Another problem is the question of the pollution of the Kootenay and Columbia rivers. I will deal with that matter later, but this is a problem that will have to be faced in the years ahead, and I think it is a problem which should be on the agenda of the minister and his senior officials so they may have the background from personal knowledge, as a result of visiting this area, before they undertake any concrete action. I hope the minister will find it possible in between his engagements on television to visit the Kootenay district. This remark applies equally to the deputy minister and some of the senior officials, because there are some growing problems which involve other departments.

Another suggestion I wish to make is this.
I think there should be increasing co-operation among the various departments, namely the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys, the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources and the Department of Agriculture, because some of these things are directly related to the development of agriculture in the area. Once again I suggest that the local people in the district should be kept informed of what the department is doing.
I think this should be undertaken in two ways. I think there should be authorized press releases. It is amazing the amount of misinformation that can be given out as a result of speculation and rumour. I have even found men coming into the district expecting employment on a certain project because of false information which has been retailed in the press and elsewhere. I do think there is a place for factual information with respect to the work being undertaken by the department, and I think this is a necessary aspect of public relations. You would be surprised to know, Mr. Chairman, that although the government of Canada is contributing a certain percentage of the cost of certain projects, because of the lack of these periodic press releases containing factual information the public is not aware of the fact that the government of Canada is investing so much money in certain developments in co-operation with provincial and municipal authorities. I do suggest that this proposal of mine should be given further consideration.
Now I am going to repeat a suggestion which I think I have made on previous occasions, and one which I think is possible. In the first instance we should like the minister to come to the district and give us a television show or even address a public meeting and meet the local people. I want to thank the minister for a most enjoyable 30 minutes recently on the Toronto program which should be called "Financial Fantasy," I enjoyed it, and every time there was a close up of the minister's face I loved looking at that cherubic expression. My old landlady said "You know, that there old fellow couldn't do any wrong. He looks too innocent". Anyway, I do hope he gives consideration to this suggestion.
These are matters of importance to local communities. The people who live in larger centres such as Vancouver, Toronto, Peterborough and places like that are possibly not so greatly affected, but when you live in a district where there are a lot of small and isolated communities near which there is considerable expenditure of public funds by this department, it has an effect on the lives of the people in those communities. I do urge that even more consultation should take place between officials of the department and local
Supply-Public Works
organizations such as chambers of commerce, farmers' institutes and, in some cases, women's institutes; because you will find that in some cases the activities of the department are affecting a beach on which the women's institute has been spending money for years as a playground for the children of the district.
When contact is made with these and other groups it should be on the basis of calling on the executive, or on the committee. I am not one who believes in trotting around seeing one or two people, regardless of political opinions, who claim to represent the opinion of the community. Very often they represent only themselves. I realize there has been a tremendous improvement in recent years, but I think this co-operation should be developed further.
Now I come to my fourth suggestion, and that is that there should be more concern shown for casual or temporary employees. This is a most unusual use of the term, because a man may be a temporary employee after he has been working for the department for 30 years. As I say, more concern should be shown for the so-called casual or temporary employees. May I illustrate this by saying we have a dredge on the Arrow lakes known as Dredge Arrow Lakes which does this work of dredging, pile driving and things of that sort. There is a crew which has been on that dredge for many years. Some of these men have worked for the department for years and years. They are very capable. They understand the operation of the dredge. In a number of cases they have refused, shall I say, more profitable employment because they have been with the department for years, they like the work, and they have a sense of loyalty to the department, a certain esprit de corps. On occasions the work of this dredge is discontinued. It was discontinued in November of this year and the men were simply laid off without reason being given. I suggest we should retain this crew of good employees in these circumstances by an arrangement of the work done on certain projects and by timing so as to make it possible for them to continue doing some work, whether it is repairs on the wharves, river bank work or something else of that kind.
I do urge that further consideration be given to providing continuous employment for men who are in reality permanent employees of the department. I do not think it is good enough that they should be ditched at the beginning of November and told there will not be anything doing until the spring. There have been occasions when men were taken from other jobs to assist with certain projects, but I think those tasks could have

Supply-Public Works
been delayed and these men used for that purpose. The number involved is not large; the total is eight or ten at the most.
When the minister replies I wish some information with respect to the policy of the department concerning the design of public buildings. I believe we can arrive at a policy which provides in every respect for the functional and the beautiful. We have had no information to date which clearly outlines the department's policy with respect to the design of certain types of buildings, certain sizes of buildings, for certain types of sites, various communities and so on. I hope the minister will give us information in that respect before his estimates are completed.
The question of the trans-Canada highway has been raised. We are all pleased that the Rogers pass section of the highway will be opened some time this year. That will be a great achievement for the department and of great advantage to the people of Canada. Could the minister give us information concerning the latest dispatches from the front? In this connection I wish to direct attention to an article in the Revelstoke Review of February 15 which is not very enthusiastic about the hon. member for Kootenay West. The editor is a prominent Social Crediter; a nice chap but very misguided. I quote:
Gunners fight glacier slides.
Gunners of 2nd field regiment Royal Canadian Horse Artillery from Winnipeg, Manitoba, have had their busiest winter yet with their program of firing at potential avalanches in Glacier national park.
The avalanche control program is a co-operative project of the Department of National Defence and the national parks branch of the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources designed to reduce avalanche danger to a minimum in the Rogers pass area where the trans-Canada highway is in its last stages of construction. The highway is expected to open in the summer of 1962.
The artillery detachment from the regular army use a 105-millimeter gun-howitzer and a 75 millimeter pack-howitzer to fire at specified potential avalanches. The gunfire either stabilizes the snow, or brings it down as a "controlled" avalanche.
It goes on to give the details of what was done in this respect. We would like a report from the minister concerning this interesting development. The minister is fortunate in having a former general as deputy minister. Years ago I had little love for generals, but I have since met one or two of whom I am very fond. The deputy minister, being a former general, should be in a position to give us the latest dispatches from the front and report on the success which this attack has achieved to date. I trust we will hear from him in this respect.
Mr. Pallet!: The N.D.P. has a love of general confusion.
[Mr. Herridge.l

I did not hear that interjection. We will soon be completing the trans-Canada highway. Others have mentioned the necessity of a second trans-Canada highway, and naturally most people support the route that would serve their district best. I am not parochial in my attitude. I always support the point of view which I think is of advantage to Canada. The hon. member for Cariboo may want the second highway to go beside his ranch. I do not go along with that point of view.
I suggest that the southern transprovincial highway in British Columbia should be a portion of the second trans-Canada highway for several sound reasons. First of all there is the population in the southern part of the province. There is also the production of the area and the tax revenues. Also it is an all weather route. I shall not speak at great length on the subject at this time. However, it is time the government gave consideration to the second trans-Canada highway. While it is doing so I trust the minister will give consideration to the many arguments that have been advanced with respect to the southern transprovincial highway in British Columbia being a part of the second trans-Canada highway.
There is another problem to which consideration should be given. Under the minister's jurisdiction there is the beneficent legislation with respect to grants to municipalities for the construction of sewage disposal plants, etc. We will have to broaden the base of this excellent legislation if we are to meet successfully the increasing problem of the pollution of our rivers and lakes across the country.
This provides a tremendous opportunity for co-operation among the federal, provincial and municipal authorities. I hope the cooperation is of such a nature that the results will be evident. It should be a co-operation which people can understand and in which they may participate in spirit. There is a growing problem on the Kootenay and the Columbia rivers caused by the increasing population. No individual industry or community is directly involved, and the problem has increased in recent years because of growing industrial development and the expanding population. The department will have to consider introducing legislation and improving existing measures to remedy the situation while it still can be remedied.
We have sewage disposal from the city of Nelson going into the Kootenay river. We have industrial waste and other limited disposal of wastes. There is industrial waste going into the river in East Kootenay. I hope my friend the hon. member for Kootenay

East is not aroused by my comments. All this waste is going into the Kootenay river. The municipalities are unable to meet the problem unaided because they lack the financial resources. I urge the department to give consideration to a study of the pollution problem on the Kootenay and Columbia rivers. Action cannot be taken without knowledge and facts. Then an effort should be made to interest the provincial government and local authorities. As a result of the cooperation among the three levels of government a solution to the problem must be found before it becomes more serious.
In connection with this problem I was interested to read in a recent issue of the Ottawa Citizen-the one containing a sketch of our recent leader-an editorial dealing with this subject:
A full-scale attack on water pollution.
This country is far from coming really to grips with the problem of pollution of its waters. Isolated steps have been taken, all of a commendable nature, but there is yet no vigorous and comprehensive national policy.
I am in complete agreement with that editorial statement.
The international joint commission has to its credit a co-operative program of several years' standing in restoring and maintaining the purity, as far as possible, of streams on both sides of the international boundary in the great lakes region.
I know from reading reports and sitting on committees of this house that the commission has done an excellent job with the co-operation of industry and municipalities in the area. I see that the hon. member for Essex East is listening to my remarks with great attention.
I always like to listen to the hon. member, even when in error.

We have the same approach in that respect. I continue:
The federal government can point to its inducements to municipalities to build sewage treatment and disposal plants; this is a constructive step and represents one of the best things the present government has done in any field.
Yet much more needs to be done. The Ottawa river is still in a disgraceful condition. This has been pointed out many times but never more forcefully or with more detailed documentation than by Mr. Gustave Prevost, chairman of the recently published Quebec water purification board, in a paper prepared for the resources for tomorrow conference last fall.
The latest body to express concern about pollution of water-and in the air and on land as well- is the health officers of British Columbia, in an appearance before the royal commission on health services.
I bring this to the attention of the minister.
Supply-Public Works
The health officers submit that Canadian municipalities-and perhaps even provinces-are unable to cope with the problem, and that it should be attacked on a national scale.
In the commons recently a private bill introduced by H. W. Herridge of Kootenay West to levy heavy penalties on industrial firms polluting interprovincial waters met the usual fate of such bills and was talked out.
Even though the Prime Minister had introduced a similar bill in 1955.
Everyone who spoke was as much opposed to pollution as to sin, but no one seemed ready to do anything.
The government itself appears content for the time being to rest on its far from adequate antipollution measure which is hoped will result in the construction of more municipal sewage disposal systems. If the measure is effective, well and good, but the industrial wastes aspect will still remain. It is doubtful whether the mere imposition of penalties is going to bring desired results.
I do urge that serious consideration be given to having a study made of the major problems with respect to water pollution across Canada with a view to approaching the provincial and municipal governments for joint action by all governments so that this very dangerous situation which will face us in the years ahead can be corrected. In this connection, Mr. Chairman, once again here is a problem that requires local participation, in that you have to have local understanding of the problem and local support for the solving of it so that municipalities and other governing bodies will receive support for any taxation measures they wish to introduce to meet the cost of these very desirable works.
That is all I have to say at the present time on item No. 1. I have a few remarks to make with respect to particular items when they come before the house, but I shall now resume my seat.

Mr. Chairman, I have a few brief remarks on item No. 1 of the estimates of the Department of Public Works. Inasmuch as the constituency of Winnipeg North Centre is in the middle of the city of Winnipeg, it is not favoured with too many public works projects, but I should like to thank the Minister of Public Works for the construction of a fine building last year which now houses the unemployment insurance commission. Although there were some difficulties with regard to the provision of public facilities, I understand that these have now been overcome.
I do not think there is anything in the estimates for the forthcoming year for the construction of further public buildings in my constituency, although there is some hope that sooner or later we may perhaps get a post office building constructed in the Weston section. However, I should like to thank the

Supply-Public Works
minister and the federal government for the announcement made last fall with regard to slum clearance in the city of Winnipeg, and in particular in my constituency. This is something that has been talked about by my predecessors in the house for the past 16 to 20 years, but nothing was ever done about it.
The fact of the matter simply is that in October of last year the federal government announced a plan to participate in a slum clearance project in Winnipeg North Centre in the amount of approximately $4 million. As I say, this is a major step forward, because in Winnipeg North Centre we have some areas that certainly deserve such treatment. I understand that the project itself still has not been approved by the provincial legislature, and so far there is no agreement between the city of Winnipeg and the province which would enable the minister to tell the house when a start can be made on the project.
I should also like to ask the minister if anything further has been done with relation to slum clearance in the area just south of the C.P.R. tracks and west of Main street. In the planning stage this was to have been the No. 1 project in slum clearance, but for some reason or other it has now become the No. 2 project. I should also like the minister to tell me, if he can, just how far negotiations have proceeded on this aspect of the matter.
I should also like to make one further point having to do with housing for our senior citizens. When we are dealing with such housing it is necessary now to go through the National Housing Act and pick out the applicable sections. I might say that Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation has done a good deal in this regard. In the city of Winnipeg many C.M.H.C. projects have been constructed which have certainly served the needs of some of our senior citizens. But the fact still remains that there is a need of accommodation for single old age pensioners, particularly for those who are just barely existing on the old age pension and have no other assets or alternative income. The C.M.H.C. projects already constructed for the benefit of senior citizens make provision for married couples and only those couples who are able to pay rent, which sometimes takes all their old age pension cheque.
I have in mind consideration of that type of construction known as hostel type accommodation. The minister is familiar with this. He has received representations from myself and other members from the city of Winnipeg with regard to the project undertaken by the aged and opportunity bureau in the city of Winnipeg two years ago. There is a crying need for it in my constituency because it contains a large low rental rooming house
[Mr. MacLean (Winnipeg North Centre).!
area where senior citizens who are single and have no relatives, exist, and I do mean exist.
The government has seen fit to do more for the old people of our country by way of old age pensions than any other government in our history, and I submit that it is time we took a look at housing for our senior citizens on a separate level entirely. Perhaps there should be a separate act with regard to housing for senior citizens, or if not a separate act there should certainly be a section in the National Housing Act dealing solely with the provision of housing for our senior citizens.
The hostel type of accommodation would fulfil a dire need, and when the minister replies I would ask him to advise me with regard to anything that has been done in the way of setting up, either under C.M.H.C. or in his department, a division to deal with this subject. I conclude by commending the minister and the government again for their direct attention after assuming power to the matter of slum clearance in the city of Winnipeg.

Mr. Chairman, I rise this morning to participate very briefly in the debate on a subject that interests a great many members of the house no matter on which side they sit, and I refer to the question of housing. I was interested in the minister's speech yesterday. I watched him as he began, and he seemed to be flushed by the effect of the rather heady wine of the personal praise of the Prime Minister-

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: My speech had not arrived.

-for his recent television extravaganza. The minister made yet another presentation to the house yesterday and, as he knows, I listened very carefully. In fact I have read his speech this morning. I believe this is an attempt to create a new image of him as a sort of great producer, now. I hope perhaps to show that this is a new interest, a new flair.
I have marked a few things in his speech upon which I should like to comment. According to page 1374 of Hansard, the minister referred in very glowing terms to the impact of house building and related industries on the national economy. He said that it had been revealed in all its sharpness and clarity by the giant forward steps taken, and so on.
I hope to be able to show that this was a period of feast or famine in the house building industry.
Further down on the same page I find the minister used a new term which sounds very well. He said:
-woven into the whole fabric of housing, bright and chromatic in its colours-

I thought perhaps yesterday I had misunderstood his language, and when he said "chromatic" I thought he said "aromatic". I think that would be a little more appropriate according to some assessments of the situation. In another sentence the minister makes reference to the lower income families in a very complimentary way so far as the government is concerned. Yet I think it can be shown that last year some 92 per cent of the people who borrowed under N.H.A. were earning more than $80 per week, which is more than the national average. I believe this statement in itself is an answer to the government's extravagant claims.
In the next sentence I find another term the minister used "most vividly impart to hon. members something of the drama of housing in Canada..." The drama of housing interests me. Here the minister shows he is not satisfied with just being an actor on T.V., as I said a moment ago; he now wants to be the producer. Another item that attracted my attention was his reference, on the following page, to the 2.5 million Canadians who now have new homes as the result of the present government's action. Well, that points up the 16 million Canadians who have houses that they acquired under more favourable interest rates and costs under the previous administrations.
I was rather intrigued by his reference further along to the unoccupied houses. The minister referred to 36 major Canadian urban centres in which there were 4,223 unoccupied houses. I know the minister's regard for figures, an interest that he displayed the other evening on television. Those figures used by the minister refer to the situation as of December 31, 1961. I should like to point to an article appearing in the Montreal Gazette just ten weeks earlier, which stated that there were 1,600 C.M.H.C. homes and 10,000 private units vacant in that area alone.
Without making any further comment, I just wanted to refer to that situation. Again, further down I find this:
-it has been necessary at the same time to maintain the lowest possible interest rate so that borrowers do not find themselves confronted by unnecessarily excessive costs for the money they have obtained.
Well, now, that is a strange observation. I should like to do something I have never done before, and that is refer to something I said in this house on an earlier occasion. I am going back to June 15 of last year, and I quote from page 6382 of Hansard:
As X mentioned earlier, today's main deterrent is not the scarcity of mortgage funds but rather the high cost of mortgage funds. In an earlier debate I dealt in some detail with this 61 per cent N.H.A. rate. Suffice it to say today that a person buying a $15,000 home over a 35 year period will pay $22,476 in Interest.
Supply-Public Works
How any one can associate that with keeping interest rates down so that borrowers will not find themselves confronted by unnecessary excessive costs for money, is indeed difficult to understand.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I think the one point that really struck me was the minister's reluctance to make a forecast of the situation for the present year. I suppose he has his reasons. I can think back to 1960, when a forecast was made by the then minister of trade and commerce to the effect that there would be 140,000 new homes in 1960. As we know, unfortunately the year ended with only 108,000 new homes started. The minister went on to use another phrase that interested me. He said there were too many imponderables. I thought to myself, what an accurate assessment of the fickle whims and fancies of some of his government colleagues.
The minister ended his speech on a very high note, and I think that reflects his broadening interest resulting from his travels. He referred to his travels in Europe and southeast Asia. As I say, he closed that section of his remarks yesterday on a very high plane indeed, for which we are all glad because, like most members of the house, I like the minister. We like him personally, and I certainly have received nothing but the best co-operation from his department, from his officials and from the minister himself. I sometimes feel a little bit sorry that he inherited the situation he did from his predecessor, the present Secretary of State for External Affairs.
I should like to begin now, Mr. Chairman, where I left off in this house last June. Having regard for the requirements of the next decade, which I am sure will demand more and more of our attention and resources, and having in mind the social and economic ramifications of such a great program, I suggested that future governments might well give consideration to giving separate cabinet status to this important area of government responsibility. In this way the housing needs of our people and the economic influences resulting from an adequate program would be assured a strong voice in government, and would not be left to another division tagged on to another department as it is at the present time.
Now, I know the minister would like, especially if this is to be an election year, to have the public believe that all is well in housing under this newly developed Progressive Conservative socialist regime. The minister, encouraged by the Prime Minister, never misses an opportunity to make extravagant claims and try to create the impression that the Tories rescued the house building industry.
1430	HOUSE OF
Supply-Public Works
What are the facts? In the past two years under this minister housing starts totalled
234.000,	while in 1955-56, the last two years of Liberal administration, housing starts totalled
265.000.	These are the facts, 32,000 fewer starts in the last two years under the Diefen-baker government. Yet, from the Prime Minister down, all government supporters have said during the past four years, from every platform where an audience could be found, that housing under the Liberal administration was at a standstill. If that be a proper description, then housing under the Tories in 1960-61 could be described as at a standstill minus 32,000.
Yesterday we had the minister pointing, as he has every right to do, to the employment resulting from housing, but on that basis there is a difference here of 80,000 fewer jobs. What better example could we find of a government misjudging the situation than to have housing, which is admittedly a good work providing program, grinding to its lowest ebb during 1960-61 when at one point over 700,000 of our people were looking for work? No amount of campaigning or campaign literature will ever get this government off the hook for such a blunder and miscalculation.
Let us examine the record further. First there was a frantic overstimulation of the house building industry by a nervous, inexperienced government, building the wrong houses in many cases for the wrong people in the wrong areas, a situation brought to the nation's attention by a prominent Canadian banker, Mr. Ashforth. This period, under the minister's predecessor, the present minister of external affairs, was described as a Tory housing binge; but following the binge comes the sobering up period, and that was handed over to the present minister which brought us to the greatest period of slack in house building, 108,000 starts in 1960, which served to aggravate the unemployment situation of 1960-61, the period of highest unemployment in our history.
Throughout this whole affair the ministry jointly must take the blame. We cannot accuse the Minister of Public Works of being solely responsible for this, not by any stretch of the imagination. The ministry talked and travelled and doodled. I just got the dictionary off the table a few minutes ago, Mr. Chairman, and I think "doodling" is the best description we can have. It says "an aimless scrawl while one's attention is engaged elsewhere," and I think this word is properly applicable to the ministry.
Under this government the period to which I have referred in the housing field has been one of the highest interest rates since the N.H.A. has been in effect. It has been a period of turning on and turning off the tap 

on mortgage funds. It has been a period of overstimulation of the house building industry, which resulted in higher costs through many inefficient would-be builders being artificially encouraged, and it has been a period of overpricing of land to keep pace with the overstimulation of the industry. It has also led to periods of slowdown. Without detracting from the number of houses built by this government during that period, may I say that in general it has been a period of high costs and uncertainty, a situation for which the government must take its full share of the blame.
I have one further observation to make of interest to Canadians. In their attempts to administer during this period, these self-styled champions of free enterprise in four years, have had to use approximately $1,500 million to support their on again off again housing program; while the former Liberal administration in an earlier period of greater economic buoyancy, with an extra drain on funds, was able to build a comparable number of houses and used only $100 million of public funds. Do you get the picture, Mr. Chairman; $1,500 million by the Tories and $100 million by the Liberals? What an example of Tory free enterprise.
Now, let us examine the present situation. After the war many small homes were built of the two bedroom style, but today the family which occupied one of these has grown and more space is required. The need for larger quarters is very real in thousands of cases across the country. The occupant of one of these homes is a prospective house buyer, but he is discouraged or unable to build or buy for several reasons which I would like to refer to briefly.
First of all, he is unable to get his equity out of the original house. Hence the need for extending N.H.A. lending facilities to assist him, and this is something we have been talking about on this side of the house for the past three years. There is another factor, and probably equally important, in that he is only paying 4.5 per cent or 5 per cent on his existing N.H.A. mortgage entered into during the days of Liberal administration. He is naturally reluctant to increase the size of the mortgage which under this administration would mean paying an increased charge of 6.5 per cent. In the back of his mind he knows that the present high interest rates are not necessarily permanent, and that is another factor. He remembers the lower interest rates of earlier days when the economy was buoyant and competition for funds was keen.
There is a further reason, and I believe a very real one. It is his lack of confidence and reluctance to take on added financial responsibility in view of this government's record

of failure to keep the economy rolling. We have seen a period of retrenchment, a recession, a slackening in job opportunities under this administration, and this is a matter of real concern to the prospective buyer when he is considering taking on new responsibilities. This government, despite increased spending and increased taxation, has not faced up to the unemployment problem, a problem which is worse in this rich young land than in any industrial nation in the free world. It is little wonder then that the prospective home buyer, despite his need for larger accommodation, is reluctant at the present time to take on added financial obligations.
The current year, 1962, without further encouragement may well be a year no better in terms of housing starts than 1961, which could be considered good only by comparison with the standstill year of 1960. We were naturally pleased by the government's effort to encourage the establishment of a secondary market for mortgages. The minister knows our feelings on this subject. For three years we have talked and argued about them in this house, and for the success they have had we are glad. If my memory serves me right something like $41 million worth have been sold. This is a small amount when we consider the amounts that are available, but when one considers the problem of disposing of mortgages at lower interest rates than those that have been disposed of, then one can have a fuller appreciation of the problem. Having taken this first little timorous step I think it is now time to give consideration to our second recommendation that envisages participation by small investors. This is something that we have talked about for a long time. I think it would have a very real effect in reaching the objectives that are so desirable.
We also noted with interest the reduction of one quarter of one per cent in the N.H.A. interest rate last fall. The minister knows our opposition to high interest rates and to the folly of his government's policies that led them to high interest rates, so he will understand me when I say that in regard to this one quarter of one per cent reduction, if ever the term "too little, too late" applied, it is here.
Last year saw another unfortunate development as a result of this government's policies and action. I refer to the Ontario sales tax. The committee will remember the scene at Massey hall, where our Prime Minister and the premier of Ontario stood arm in arm. The Prime Minister was introduced as the man who was going to give Ontario its just dues. When we look back to see what he has given Ontario; he has given that province a do it 26207-1-91

I should now like to say a few words about urban redevelopment and our hard pressed municipalities. The Canadian problem is not only to clear up slum areas, but as I see it it is also to prevent slums developing whenever possible. This calls for more planning, more land assembly, more municipal planning, more technical assistance. Here I return to where I began. This is the sort of thing that could be carried out even better with the full attention of a ministry of housing. This is a tremendous problem and as such it is a great challenge, especially against the background of the financial need of our municipalities.
I should like to refer to some public financing statistics published by the dominion bureau of statistics, which point out that in 1960 the municipalities incurred a net deficit of more than double the 1956 level; in 1956 the defiicit was $295 million and in 1960 it was $506 million.
The federal government contributes to the cost of blight areas only if the land is used for housing development. Often, however, a good, sound renewal project requires other kinds of development. A new Liberal approach would be to contribute to the cost of clearing land for any appropriate use and would include sharing the cost of renewing and improving basic services such as water, sewers and streets in the development areas.
The Liberal policy for municipal development would operate as part of a national development program. For the last four years the Liberal party has recommended the establishment of a municipal loan fund. This fund would be organized in consultation with provincial and municipal representatives. It would not conflict with existing sources of capital, and it would provide loans for sound municipal improvements of which the provincial governments approve but for which capital is unobtainable on reasonable terms from existing Canadian sources. These loans would create new jobs all across Canada.
To sum up, Mr. Chairman, I would say that the Liberal approach in this municipal loan


fund program, in co-operation with the provinces, would provide money for municipal services and would do a great deal for housing in this country. We would increase the federal government's contribution to slum clearance; we would broaden the federal government's contribution to all kinds of urban renewal costs; we would provide special aid to municipalities and distressed areas; we would provide capital for rural redevelopment plans, and in co-operation with the provinces we would increase the construction of low rental homes.

Thank you, Mr. Chairman. However, I want to be fair with the minister. If his department lacks enthusiasm, vision and ideas, I am not ready to put upon him alone the burden of his failure.
When a man has done everything he could, when he has reached the limits of his capacities, his failure is noted but the blame cannot be cast upon him.
We must be fair. It may be that the Minister of Public Works, having been connected with the courts of law for many years, could have been an excellent solicitor general. I should like to say a few words on the trans-Canada highway as part of the joint projects. Yesterday, when the hon. member for Levis (Mr. Bourget) had the floor, some Conservative members raised the question of joint programs. They tried to show a difference between our stand now concerning those joint programs and the stand we had in the past. Well, I wish at this point to put on record a statement by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) which was published in Le Soleil of November 7, 1961:
The Liberal leader said he thought the federal government should withdraw from joint plans of a permanent nature. That suggestion applies especially in the field of social security.
Upon ending its financial participation in those programs, the federal government should compensate the provinces by giving them more room in the field of direct taxation and by adding equalization in order not to increase their financial burden. Such a system does not mean however that the Liberal party will not put forward in the future any new joint program, but it means that those new plans, if they require a permanent and rather regular expenditure, will not be in effect for more than five years before being handed over to the exclusive control of the provinces.
Mr. Chairman, having read that statement of the Leader of the Opposition, I should like to read also into the record a sentence from the speech made by the present premier of 26207-1-92

the province of Quebec at the federal-provincial conference last year. That quotation may be found on page 35 of the proceedings of that conference. I quote Mr. Jean Lesage:
In our opinion, this situation has become undesirable. The existing joint programs have played a stimulating role in the economic and social development of the country; in several cases, they have supplemented provincial initiatives. But these programs are now sufficiently well established on the provincial scale to enable the federal government to cease taking part in them and to vacate these fields. The federal government should be prepared to accept this request. Obviously, in such a case, it would be necessary to compensate the provinces fully for the additional financial responsibilities assumed by them. This financial compensation should take the form of additional taxation rights specifically reserved for the provincial governments and of correspondent equalization payments. If this were done, each province would be free to use its revenues as it sees fit in the fields of jurisdiction that belong to it.
I hope, Mr. Chairman, that our position has now been made clear, as well as that of the government of the province of Quebec, about those joint plans.
I should like to add this. It is quite obvious that for those works or undertakings of a national character, we must consider both the constitutional aspect of the situation and the public welfare.
No one will deny that a trans-Canada highway was essential to this country, that such a project involved provincial problems and that it could not be undertaken otherwise than on the basis of federal-provincial cooperation. That is my view, as it has always been. There is nothing new in the fact that when those plans are set up they must in no way be permanent, and that the sooner we get out of them the better.
Mr. Chairman, I should now like to draw the conclusion that naturally evolves from the consideration of those estimates by saying this. The government is not taking this department seriously. It does not give the Minister of Public Works, in the present circumstances, the important and essential part that should be his. And finally, it is quite obvious that the government has no plan nor any specific policy to solve the economic problems we are now facing.

Mr. Chairman, in reply to the hon. member-and I will only be very brief and will not trade insults with him-the actual total expenditures in the Department of Public Works for 1955-56 to 1956-57 inclusive averaged $82.1 million; for 1956-58 and 1960 to 1961 inclusive they averaged

Supply-Public Works
$204.7 million. No matter how you insult or exaggerate, the figures speak for themselves.
In housing it is the same record. If in 1960 and 1961 the figures were not as high as before, it is because in the two years 1958 and 1959 they reached the enormous and astronomical number of 164,632 starts in 1958, and in 1959 the figure was 141,345. As a matter of fact I have gone into those figures before to indicate that the housing under our administration so far exceeded the housing under the Liberal administration that it is only an hon. member such as comes from Maisonneuve-Rosemont who would even have the audacity to get up and compare the figures. No matter how he uses that virulent tongue of his and no matter how he dishes it out, the departmental figures do not lie and they speak for themselves. Is it not about time that we had an end to all this nonsense?

First, I should like to take this opportunity to congratulate the minister on the excellent showing that has been made in this past year. I would be very remiss if I did not also pass along my thanks to the officials of the department for their assistance during the year.
I should like to support the hon. member for Kootenay West in what he had to say about the contentious question of sewage disposal. At the present time this problem is not too serious in my area but with the expansion that is going on I can see that within a very few years we shall be facing the same situation. Likewise, I should like to mention my support for a southern trans-Canada highway. This will be classed as our number two highway. We have just about completed the first highway and with any luck it should be opened this year. What we need now is a trans-Canada highway running through the southern section of the province of British Columbia.
I should like to bring the minister's attention to some of our problems in British Columbia; they may be a little different from those which have been raised so far. I realize that British Columbia is not too popular a province at the present time-

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: It is with this government.

We are going to make some changes. Our problem at the present time has to do with flooding conditions, and I will begin at the top end of the constituency of East Kootenay. East Kootenay has generally been considered as the lost lamb of the province of British Columbia; it was too far from Victoria to be considered, and it was too far away from Ottawa to be known about. My difficulty at the present time is to present the facts about the needs

of East Kootenay and bring them to the attention of this committee. First I should like to begin at the northern end of the district where we have a flooding problem. It is in the municipality of Golden, which is steadily expanding. The village of Golden is situated on an ancient flood plain or small delta, mainly built up from materials brought down by the Kicking Horse river to its confluence with the Columbia river. It consists of firmly packed coarse gravel overlaid by a thin mantle of silt. As such, in an area with limited land suitable for building purposes, the delta of the Kicking Horse river has become a valuable townsite building area. On the other hand, the Columbia river, north and south of Golden flows in a swampy silt filled valley, where the waters easily seek new channels and courses. In the environ of Golden the river maintains a permanent position along the rim rock of the west side of the valley. Though this advantage exists, making it possible to build a town at Golden, the condition is in delicate balance. During the three months of summer freshet the Columbia spills over its channel on to part of the townsite, and the water table rises over a large area to an undesirable height.
Flooding in this area has become periodic in recent years and the situation is gradually becoming worse. The main cause would appear to be the influence of the Kicking Horse river upon the free flow of the Columbia river. The alluvial deposits, mostly pebbles and round rock up to six inches in diameter, spill into the Columbia and have built up bars and shoals for several hundred yards downstream. This action has slowed the free flow of the river so that the Columbia is filling its channel with gravel and silt above the confluence with the Kicking Horse river.
Another factor which congests the flood waters of the Columbia in the environ of Golden is a narrow reef of bed rock which crosses the river a few hundred yards below the Kicking Horse junction and which outcrops on the east bank of the Columbia in the form of a small obstructive island.
We have made several recommendations to the departments concerned, both federal and provincial, but so far we have not been able to get any government to accept the responsibility for alleviating this flooding condition. I have with me today a brief submitted by the people of Golden. We are asking for the assistance of the government, and the question that arises is: which government is responsible? Is it the provincial government, is it the federal government or is it both? I feel it is up to this government as the senior government in the dominion of

Canada to take the lead in this matter and, if necessary, to put it on a fifty-fifty basis. Let us do this so that the people in the area can be assured that they are not going to be flooded out year after year.
A similar situation exists in the village of Athalmer further down the Columbia river. Streams running into the Columbia bring down shale and rocks, and have built up the river to such an extent that in some cases the water is actually running up hill. This can easily be seen. The people in this area have built up a certain amount of equity in their homes, businesses, motels, and so on, and the problem today is to prevent the flooding which threatens the existence of much of this property each spring.
I am going further down the valley, and we now come to the Kootenay river. Similar flooding conditions are encountered there, especially where the Goat river runs into the Kootenay. This government is very interested in the Kootenay because it will be part of our power project as soon as the necessary arrangements can be concluded.
I have brought up these three points as a matter of interest and I should like to ask the minister if he will consider taking action on a fifty-fifty basis. As I said earlier, I believe we should take the lead in bringing this matter to a satisfactory conclusion. I notice that a proposal has been made to spend approximately $63 million this year on a flood control program around greater Winnipeg and that the federal government is to pay approximately 60 per cent of the cost. A similar plan was undertaken a few years ago when Vancouver was experiencing flooding difficulties. Many millions were spent in order to control these floods. It seems to me that although the large centres are provided for, the smaller centres are not being given the consideration to which they are entitled.
I do not think there is anything I should like to add at the present time. I should be pleased to discuss this matter either with the minister or with his officials to see whether this problem can be approached in such a way that the people of this area can be assured that their land, their property and their belongings are not going to be washed out during the freshet season. I have received numerous letters from the department in which it is claimed that this is not a national emergency. Believe me, when a man sees his home and his business going down the river he knows it is a national emergency for him.

time to my hon. friend's area-there is no possible way in which the Department of Public Works could intervene.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to compliment the minister on being such a nice, co-operative gentleman with whom to deal during the years he has held his present office. At the same time I think the minister is a complex fellow. We have had two exhibitions of his complexity within the last week. The first was on television the other night. The program was thoroughly enjoyed by everyone I spoke to who had seen it. The second demonstration was the performance we witnessed in the house yesterday. As a result I find it almost impossible to understand why, when he is such a capable fellow privately, the minister must try to make a public idiot of himself.
And succeeds.
The minister appears to have a split personality. His schizophrenia is so extensive that I have known him to privately apologize for public insults.
