speechtext: That will be the day.

In any event I do not think I should pursue this subject or I shall be guilty of indulging in the same language that the minister used yesterday, which I do not think is in the best interests of the discussion in this committee.
Yesterday he attempted to drown the committee with figures. He attempted to lay claim on behalf of the government for every house and building constructed in Canada by federal governments, provincial governments, municipal governments, co-operatives, school boards, credit unions, private citizens, and so on. In view of his television performance I would not be surprised if the minister had a count made of all the beaver houses built last year in order to place a value on them and claim them, too. I do not wish to take away from the minister any credit of which he is deserving. I am perfectly willing to admit there has been a marked improvement in his department, particularly compared with his record during the first year he served in that portfolio. Speaking in this house at that time I remember pointing out that the minister regretfully did not follow the excellent example of his illustrious predecessor in the department. The first year there was a considerable falling away and I am pleased to see the minister is now attempting to take up the slack. I think it would be advantageous if he were to spend less effort patting himself on the back and more energy attempting to determine what remains to be done.
There are three matters in which he should take more interest in the future than he

Supply-Public Works
appears to have taken in the past. The first is the shameless exploitation of labour in the housing field, especially that coming under his jurisdiction. There has been a shameless exploitation of immigrant labour.
I fully realize that the minister and government members may say that a large part of this matter comes under provincial jurisdiction. That is true but the fact remains that in the public mind and in the eyes of the people involved the federal government is responsible and will receive the blame for it. People consider that because these houses are being built with the taxpayers' money the government must assume some of the responsibility and manifest a keener interest to ensure that these conditions are corrected.
Another aspect of this problem has been brought to my attention as it affects my own and other ridings where people building houses through various means are attempting to evade the responsibilities which our society requires employers to assume. Instead of letting out contracts, some are attempting to evade responsibility such as that of providing for workmen's compensation, unemployment insurance and so on. Again in the eyes of the public and those concerned the blame is laid squarely at the door of the minister and the government. Even when you explain the federal government is not directly involved, people take the position that it is federal government money that is being expended and the government should ensure that these conditions do not prevail. This will reflect on the federal government until the minister shows more interest than he has in the past.
Another way of looking at it is this. If the minister wishes to take credit for every building constructed in Canada he will also have to accept the responsibility and blame arising from any problems in the construction field.
Another matter in which the minister should express more interest is that of the calibre of the housing being built across the country particularly when public funds are Involved directly or indirectly. There is a growing list of complaints in this regard. People are becoming increasingly critical of the calibre of material being used in buildings. They do not want the building to collapse before the mortgage is cleared off.
On two occasions, through the present minister and his predecessor, I have had to call for investigations into public housing built with public funds in my area. On both occasions while the construction appeared to meet minimum standards I can assure the minister the people blamed the federal government and were far from satisfied with the calibre of materials.

It is significant that although the minister had extended time yesterday to present his estimates neither of the points I have raised was mentioned during the course of his remarks.
A third matter deserving more attention is that of slum clearance. No mention was made of present or future plans in this field. The minister outlined the department's plans for the construction of public buildings, post offices, harbours, bridges, and wharves across the country but gave no indication of recognition of the problem of slum clearance let alone mentioning any plans to deal with it.
With that in mind I wish to read from the daily Star of June 3, 1961 an article entitled "Ottawa Should Lead" which accuses the minister of doing little more than lecturing the municipalities in this regard, and knowing the minister that is perhaps a correct assessment. The article reads:
Scoldings don't clear any slums, not even when the scoldings come from Canada's public works minister himself.
In Halifax this week, Mr. David Walker complained that Canadian municipalities were "not making nearly enough progress" in getting rid of slums and halting the spread of blight. He said that Ottawa offered "generous assistance" to the municipalities for these purposes, but the municipalities weren't making full use of it.
Then it goes on to say:
But the municipalities know from experience- for example, Toronto with Moss park-that being offered this kind of assistance is one thing: actually getting it is another. Because Ottawa has a big financial commitment in projects of this nature, Ottawa tightly regulates them and is painfully slow to approve them-if and when It does, In fact, approve them.
The proof of this legislation, as of any other, Is in what it accomplishes. For all the years that slum clearance and public housing have been on Ottawa's statute books, scarcely anything has been done to clear slums or to build public housing. (For the last ten years, construction of public housing in Canada has averaged fewer than 800 units a year.)
The trouble is not just in one quarter, but all along the federal-provincial-municipal line-too little in the way of leadership; too much in the way of governmental and intergovernmental complexities.
As for leadership, it should come mainly from Ottawa, which is the main source of money and authority in this field. Rather than rail at the municipalities, let Mr. Walker rally them to the cause of self-improvement.
I have spoken on many occasions in the house about the blight of slums on our society in every city and town in our country, and I do not intend to go into the details at this time. But I should like to point out once more that slums are responsible for enormous costs, for crime, social problems and degradation for fire traps, sickness, unemployment and additional welfare costs. Until such time as the federal government really takes the lead in this field and gives some leadership

to the provinces and municipalities in the form of a long term program we will not have met the problem. It is no use just taking one area, tackling the problem, meeting it there and thinking the job is done because while you are doing that slums are growing up all around you. This is not something you can do once and forget about it. It is a long term project. That is the only way the problem can be met, and the costs involved would be more than offset by the savings in other fields if and when the problem is met. Before the debate ends I hope we will hear something from the minister with regard to this field. I think he would be much better advised to spend his energies in this field rather than in a back-patting exhibition such as we saw yesterday.

First of all, I should like to compliment the minister. He is one of the best we have ever had at Ottawa. He has done a great deal for the region from which I come. The people there did not know anything about housing until he became the minister but now we are getting plenty of houses. Let a Liberal, a Social Crediter or what have you run in my riding and he will see what the people who live there think. The minister has done a real job. We have a suburban development with good houses and people are living in the houses they really want.
But that is not what I want to talk about. I want to talk about a road to provide means of communication for one of the most beautiful towns you ever saw, the town of McBride. The town nestles against the Rocky mountains but there is no road out. There is a highway six miles away which stops abruptly. I have spoken to the Department of Public Works and tried to get some action to have the road finished. Thousands of people live in that beautiful country, one of the richest parts of Canada. I hear talk about the countryside around Ottawa and in Quebec. You have not seen anything until you have seen McBride. The people are prosperous but they are cooped up against Mount Robson. Any of you who have traveled west by the C.N.R. know that the train stops on the way through the Rockies so that the passengers can look at the mountains and the guest camp that has been there for years. It was there when I was a child.
There are ranches in that area, plenty of timber and beautiful dairy farms. When you get a chance to go west you should take a look at McBride. People from the United States are coming in there. We Canadians seem to be asleep because the Americans are buying land there. There is an influx of settlers from the United States at the present time.
Supply-Public Works
As I say, it is magnificent dairy country but we need a road so that people can go to Edmonton or through to Prince Rupert. I am not going to waste the whole afternoon talking about this matter. I hope the minister will take a look at the situation and see that we get a road, because we need it badly. Talk about Newfoundland, Ontario or Quebec; here is a wonderful place, but without a road- and you have got to have roads in that country. You cannot go through there with an automobile at all. Forty years ago work was being done on the railroad but there has been no advance so far as a road for automobiles is concerned.
When I first came here I thought I would have no trouble getting a road. I have not succeeded yet, but I am not going to waste good time by talking all afternoon because the minister knows the problem and I am sure he will do something for us. As I say, he is the best public works minister we have had for many a day.

Mr. Chairman, I want to ask the minister some questions which he can answer when he replies. First of all, I should like to ask him if there is any chance in the immediate future of a reduction in the interest rate on N.H.A. mortgage loans. When the minister announced the reduction from 6J per cent to 6i per cent he put on record the amount of the saving to the home owner paying off a mortgage.
I maintain that the mortgage rate is too high at the present time and I think the minister will probably agree with that. However, I believe he said yesterday that mortgage money was being obtained at a reasonable rate. When the Minister of Finance and other members opposite were in the opposition I have a vivid recollection of hearing them lament in long speeches in the house about the high rate of interest on N.H.A. loans when the rate at that time was in fact 5| per cent. When the rate was increased to 5| per cent they really became frothy about it. They claimed they were speaking for those people who were paying on mortgages, the little man who was paying off his mortgage.
Members of the government party patted the minister on the back when he reduced the interest rate from 6J to 6J per cent. Under the former government by far the great majority of N.H.A. mortgage loans were made at 5J per cent, but under this government the great majority have been made at the rate of 6j per cent over a 25 year term.
I might say that the mortgages carrying a 5J per cent interest rate were for a term of 20 years.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to speak briefly on item 1 and mention what we regard as an urgent problem in Canada, the need for community growth. We believe that there must be a responsible and well conceived national plan which will help municipal development. It would appear, sir, that some years ago the then leader of the opposition, Mr. Diefenbaker, felt this to be of importance.
I have been checking back on some of the statements that were made in 1957. The Globe and Mail of April 26, 1957, quotes Mr. Diefenbaker as saying:
We cannot face complacently the fact that we have rising tax bills, rising debt both provincially and municipally.
In his opening campaign speech on April 25, 1957, one of the arguments which he made was:
We believe there can be no national unity in this nation until there is a realization that the federal-provincial matters have handcuffed the provinces of this nation; have denied the municipalities adequate sources of revenue; have placed the provinces and the municipalities in a position where they cannot discharge their constitutional responsibilites.
Then, on April 26, 1957, a Canadian Press report in the Winnipeg Free Press indicated that Mr. Diefenbaker pledged to work out new tax sharing arrangements with the provinces which would strengthen Canada's federal system and give provinces and municipalities the funds to carry out their responsibilities.
Probably there is no area of government labouring under greater difficulty at the present time than our municipal governments. We all know that there are plenty of useful things waiting to be done in this field. I live in an old part of Canada which was developed many years ago. It is along perhaps what could become the most beautiful riverfront in the world, with a community extending pretty well from Kingston to Cornwall, all of which was developed in the very early pioneering days. With some sort of assistance much could be done to improve living conditions in that part of the country, particularly at a time when we have an urgent unemployment problem.
Mr. J. J. Deutsch, speaking on Canada's economic problems in the winter edition of the Queen's Quarterly mentions the fact that the first half of 1961 indicates an average rate of unemployment of about 7.5 per cent of the labour force. It is clear from this article, and other articles published by economists, that during the past five years the Canadian labour force has grown twice as rapidly as in the preceding five year period. These are conditions which this administration has to face, and the problems are not going to end there
Supply-Public Works
because the projection appears to indicate that the expansion in the Canadian labour force over the next five years will be equally as large as in the last five years, and here to compound the problem is automation.
If you are really serious about recovery, and we believe recovery can take place with foresight, thought and direction, then serious attention must be given to the problems of municipal governments as well as those of provincial governments. This seems to be a need which is quoted by a great many publications. The Listening Post of February, 1962, which is the organ of the Canadian Federation of Mayors and Municipalities, asks a question which I think would not have been asked a few decades ago, perhaps not even 10 years ago. Its editorial is titled "What will the federal government do about municipal borrowing" and it says:
In the fulfilment of this need-for public transit, water supply, sewage disposal, roads, bridges, schools, hospitals, recreation facilities and the renewal of blighted areas in the central cores of our cities and towns-there exists one of the greatest potential opportunities for increasing the employment of Canadian plant capacity and Canadian manpower in the years ahead. Surely, in any well-conceived government policy, one of the nation's primary efforts should be focused on such basic programs of development in our cities and towns.
The editor of the paper indicates that this would of course be beneficial to all segments of the nation's economy, and it is sound and responsible, particularly because it is largely self-liquidating. He speaks of borrowing being "an indivisible responsibility" and says:
The chief obstacle to community development is not the reluctance of senior governments to make outright grants to local authorities. It is the lack of co-operation among the three levels of government in examining together the whole range of their capital requirements and in arranging the necessary borrowing.
It is the problem of paying. How are these municipalities going to pay for the things we know should be done in each of our towns and cities in Canada, and which can be done with a little bit of help? What these municipalities are asking for now is the full and continuing co-operation of the federal government in mobilizing the capital needed for such works, and that is why the comments made from this side of the house are so germane to the growth problems facing the local municipalities.
The N.H.A. amending legislation relating to sewers is the kind of thing for which we commend the minister and his department. We know this is important and we can see the results of it in small towns and cities. However, this major step in the right direction has got to be extended to cover a good many

other basic needs such as roads, subways, bridges, water supplies and conservation projects. It is not a policy of handouts which is being sought. It is the mobilization of capital as a national responsibility and this is the place where we must make this demand understood and known.
It is the attitude of the Liberal party that loans from a municipal loan fund in Ottawa would create new jobs all across Canada and will help to get our economy moving again on sound projects. The improved community services which we need are largely the responsibility of the municipalities and most of our municipalities have adequate plans for further development. In the area which I represent we have the community of Westport where it would be of great benefit to have better dock facilities. The city of Brockville, the town of Gananoque and the village of Athens all have plans for water supplies, schools and so on, and these projects could be implemented if there were a possibility of these municipalities borrowing at some advantageous rate.
In my riding I have been concerned to see that we have not used the winter works program in the fullest sense that might be possible, but I And it is simply impossible because the municipalities are stretched to the limit in their expenditures and cannot go beyond them.
The January, ,1962, edition of Local Finance, which is published by the Canadian tax foundation, a wise and helpful organization for citizens who are interested in better government has an article dealing with "The changing pattern of responsibilities". It says that what were once thought to be municipal responsibilities are no longer thought to be simply that. This article indicates that most of the essential local services which originally were the responsibility of local governments alone can no longer be precisely defined, and that government action in response to an increasing public demand for more government services and for better standards of performance for existing services has served to obscure the division of responsibility between governments.
When one studies what local governments do today in their executive and administrative problems in fire protection, law enforcement, street lighting, public works, streets, bridges, roads, sanitation, waste and in many health services and social welfare agencies, and add to that the obligations of education and recreational facilities and the problem of debt charges and utilities, their appropriation reserves for all the contingencies that are necessary with respect to uncollectable taxes and accounts receivable and property acquired for taxes, we see the great burden


placed on this level of local government in country and urban places in the provinces.
Referring to the winter, 1961, edition of Queen's Quarterly, and an article called "Urban Communities" written by Stewart Fyfe, the author talks about the expansion of the urban community, which is of course the principal reason why there has been this great increase of debt on our local governments.
Inevitably we see new demands on municipal government to provide new services and to raise the standards of existing services. We see the growth of our communities, a growth beyond the boundaries that existed five or ten years ago. In the United States the complexity and scale of the problems of urban growth have brought suggestions that the federal government establish a department of urban affairs. While suggestions have been made in Canada that the federal government should devote more attention to urban problems, there has been no suggestion of such a department being established. That is why we look to this genial and dedicated minister to solve these problems. He has told us of his efforts and interests and we have evidence of this. We know that this is the department and the place where we must properly raise these demands before the country.
We have to take a new look at urban development. We know that if real action is to be taken to improve this unemployment situation, it has to be done with the assistance of Ottawa; it is not enough simply to pass it on to the provinces.
A few days ago I was speaking to a man who had considerable experience of unemployment in the 1930's. He was discussing unemployment in the 1930's and comparing it with the situation today. He said that one of the great cushioning effects that we have in the 1960's to a serious unemployment situation-which has become aggravated, particularly in the last two years-is the fact that with our system of unemployment insurance people do not travel, and therefore we do not have them riding freight trains and hitchhiking across the country in one manner or another. We do not find, therefore, the long queues of men gathered for assistance and relief, because they are kept and contained in their own areas.
However, if we had something like 719,000 people last year, and 609,000 a few days ago looking for work-and we know that in our own areas this work problem is very serious-then surely this is the place and the department to whom we must look for assistance with respect to an expanded public works program.

I have found it difficult to believe that in an area as wealthy as the one I have the honour to represent,-from Cornwall to Kingston-we have pockets that are serious indeed with respect to the extent of unemployment. The unemployment situation in Cornwall is perhaps a special case, but it is frightening in its size. Prescott is very, very bad when we consider that the average unemployment last year was over 800 people in a town of that size. I would indicate to the committee, sir, that the unemployment figure reached 15.5 per cent of the population.
Gananoque is one of the most attractive little towns in the country, and yet we have had an increasing unemployment situation. It has increased regularly from 1959 to a degree that is alarming, but at the same time there are many things that need to be done in Gananoque and the local government knows what these things are.
We see even with this somewhat stagnant condition of our economy the "awesome appetite" as it has been described, of the towns and cities. The author J. Campbell Merrett takes a look at urban development in "Canadian Chartered Accountant", volume 78, 1961 and speaks of the wanton wastefulness of agricultural land, the deplorable destruction of rural amenties and the unnecessarily expensive servicing of municipal undertakings.
This problem must be dealt with, and there is no place where direction and guidance can be given better than from this particular department in a broad sharing of responsibility and effort. We look to this department for that quality of leadership.
I was reading on the microfilm a few moments ago an article in the Financial Post of September 13, 1961 entitled "Are we really trying to get rid of slums." S. L. Buckwold, who was president of the Canadian Federation of Mayors and Municipalities, argued a very strong case in 1960 before the Senate manpower committee and said that city planners and officials agree that N.H.A. is not nearly generous enough; that all major Canadian cities and many towns are suffering from a condition of "suburban sprawl" and "centre town blight". This problem could well be given more attention.
Our Minister of Public Works said at that time, as reported in the Financial Post of September 30, 1961:
I do not think enough use is being made of the very generous provisions of the N.H.A.
I wonder whether the minister can now report a more favourable use of the provisions of the N.H.A. Are these provisions sufficiently generous, or is the judgment of Mr. Buckwold correct when he says they are not?

Mr. K. Grant Crawford, in a study on the aspects of provincial-municipal relations says this:
-With increased financial assistance from the provinces came increased supervision and increased direction. .. They-
He was speaking of local municipalities:
-have seen that ever increasing provincial contributions will mean loss of local control and at the same time have been forced by their financial plight to make persistent appeals to the province for more and more assistance.
I think there is a genuine concern on the part of some of our municipalities right now lest they become too dependant upon provincial governments. They want to grow; they want to develop. They have at their helm and in their local councils, I know, some of the best brains we have available in our communities. Sometimes it is easier to get a good man to serve on a municipal council than it is to have him run for provincial or federal office. We have many competent, able and dedicated people prepared to give hundreds of hours in the year to thinking out wise developments at the municipal level, but they need assistance.
Mr. Crawford says:
To accomplish these purposes the municipalities must not be merely agencies of a higher level of government-
That, sir, is not what we are suggesting at this point.
To resume the quotation. The municipalities-
-rather must have ultimate responsibility within their sphere of jurisdiction and must have a sphere of jurisdiction sufficiently broad to make them seem significant to the citizens and thus attract into public service competent men and women in both elective and appointive offices.
I must say that over the past number of years we have seen excellent local government in the areas I represent. I know that these people have given earnest thought to development and improvements. I hope they can be encouraged by the kind of assistance at the federal level which I have suggested.
Mr. John Pratt spoke about Canada's centenary in an article in Maclean's magazine recently. He said: Let's clean up our littered countryside. He was referring to what Canada might hope for, and he suggested that there was nothing better we could do than to clean up our towns and cities and beautify this country.

To this, I subscribe.
One thing which can help toward the beautification of an area is the presence of suitable public works, and we look forward in the town of Brockville to the federal building, provision for which I find in these estimates. I thank the minister for the co-operation and the courtesy extended to the opposition member for Leeds by his department and by some of the kind and helpful members of his staff.
The importance of this building to our community is very great. Architects have been doing things in Canada which give us hope that there may be a revitalising of many of our cities. The federal building at Brockville

She speaks of the importance to a community of a building the size of the federal building which we are anticipating, as well as the importance of a park area. We are fortunate that through the recent beneficence of the Hon. Arthur C. Hardy we are to have a beautifully landscaped piece of open space on the river. You have not been in Burnaby.
Perhaps the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam would join us. We would certainly like to see him there, too.

I do not intend to be very long Mr. Chairman. However, I am a little disturbed to note that the total proposed expenditure outlined to us in the estimates of the Department of Public Works reveals a decline exceeding $4 million.
I should like to think that this government would use, as one of its instruments of stabilizing the Canadian economy, the Department of Public Works. We still have a regrettably high measure of unemployment in our country. Economic activity needs every stimulant we can possibly find at this time. I feel this is the wrong time for a government to reveal a decline in expenditures in the field of public works. I believe that this department is one of the most important instruments the government has at its disposal to regulate the economy. At a time of business expansion I believe a decrease in expenditure on the part of the Department of Public Works might well be warranted. However, at a time when our economy is either declining or stagnating, I believe that an increase in the expenditures of this department would serve a very useful purpose. In the light of the willingness of the government to incur huge budgetary deficits I cannot understand why the estimates now before us should indicate an expenditure less

than the expenditure of a year ago. I believe, as I said before, that a decrease in the proposed expenditures of the department as a whole is not, in existing circumstances, in line with the best interests of our nation. I noticed the very limited proposals in regard to public buildings. I recommend to the minister that a careful examination be made of the rentals being paid by the federal government for buildings owned by private individuals or corporations. I do not recommend that these necessarily be replaced by new buildings but I do know of a few instances where the interests of the government and the taxpayers would be well served if the existing premises were purchased upon expiration of the leases that now obtain. The government is paying fantastic rentals in ever so many cases and the interests of the taxpayers are not well served. The possibilities of purchasing existing premises or erecting new buildings ought to be explored. I believe the problem I now raise warrants the appointment of a special investigator, if necessary, to carefully review each and every instance where the Canadian government pays rent.

In dealing with harbours and rivers I have difficulty distinguishing between the responsibilities of the Minister of Public Works and his colleague the Minister of Transport. I may be completely out of line in saying this. I notice there is a division in the minister's department called the harbours and rivers engineering services. I am happy to note that within recent months the Minister of Transport and the Secretary of State for External Affairs-I hope the minister can spare a moment to listen to the complimentary remarks I wish to make-have lent a sympathetic ear to the proposal that an engineering survey be conducted to determine the feasibility of a canal being built along the ancient river bed of the Fraser to connect the Pitt river to Burrard inlet. I know that representations have been made to the minister in this regard by a number of his colleagues one of whom has given great assurances to the citizens back home.
I do not wish to publicly endorse the canal project which lately has been labelled the Kilmer canal. Miss Jane Kilmer was my opponent representing the Conservative party in a recent federal election. I admire her integrity and the useful service she has rendered the people of my constituency for

many years. I wish her continued success in her efforts on behalf of the community as a whole. I know that many years ago a close relative of hers first proposed the canal. We have had assurances that the federal government is prepared to undertake an engineering survey in line with the recommendation of the Fraser river board in 1945 indicating such a survey might well be warranted.
I speak for people of all shades of political opinion when I say I hope this request that has been made by so many organizations in the constituency will be taken seriously. This is not a political football. If the canal is proved feasible it will be of tremendous benefit to the province of British Columbia and particularly the lower mainland.
I hope the minister after adequate consultation with the Secretary of State for External Affairs, who knows every road if indeed not every little alley in the area, will ensure that the feasibility of this project will be explored and that we will have a feasibility study and a detailed and scientific report. I am not advocating that a specific sum be spent on the canal. I am not prepared to endorse this project but I do feel that the potentialities are so great that the minister should heed the advice of the Secretary of State for External Affairs and make sure that a full engineering report will be available very shortly.
In the matter of housing I noted with interest yesterday the remarks of the hon. member for Hamilton South when he spoke on these estimates. He referred to activities under the National Housing Act with regard to limited dividend housing. We regret that in British Columbia there has been practically no action. As a matter of fact, I believe I can safely say that within the last three or four years there has been no action whatsoever under this particular section of the National Housing Act.
The basic reason is obvious. The permissible returns to the investor are below the earnings that can be obtained by the purchase of government bonds. I happen to be involved in housing in our province and I have had a number of regrettable experiences where a lot of housing might have been constructed if we could have interested individuals and corporations in the limited dividend housing section of the act. The limits that now prevail under the terms of the act are such as not to encourage investors to take any interest in this aspect.
I should like the government to reconsider this matter carefully. I do not like high interest rates and in principle am opposed to them. However, when the government offers

bonds that yield a higher return than an investment under the National Housing Act which involves a certain degree of risk and returns a maximum yield lower than that provided by bonds, I believe that the government might be warranted in reconsidering the existing legislation.
There is another matter I wish to raise. I notice there is an additional vote with respect to water supply for Churchill, Manitoba. When we are spending the taxpayers' money on this project I hope that the installation of the new services will be of benefit to the citizens of Churchill generally and not merely to those in the military camps in that area.
So far as the national capital commission is concerned, I ought to be the last person in the world to advocate that citizens be limited in their right to self-determination. I am not now speaking for my party but only for myself. I am afraid my own personal conviction is that, in the light of the heavy contribution made by the taxpayers of all of Canada and considering that the city of Ottawa belongs to all Canadians, the local civic administration has shown itself repeatedly as being so thoroughly incompetent that the government would be entitled to take a very close look at the situation to see whether or not, in the interests of national pride and in the interests of protecting the investment in their national capital being made by the taxpayers of Canada as a whole, it might be advisable for the government of Canada to establish a department or commission to operate the civic affairs of the city of Ottawa. I have been in many cities of Canada and I have yet to see a more disgraceful civic administration.

speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. C-16, to amend the Canadian Elections Act (Age of voters).
He said: Mr. Speaker, the house has been so agreeable on three separate occasions now to extending the franchise to a group of people who live in the northern part of the

Canada Elections Act
country, that I am quite sure it will be equally agreeable in giving passage to this bill in order that another group of people in the country may have the franchise extended to them. I am talking of that group of people who are between the ages of 18 and 21. The bill before us has the one principle of extending the right to vote in federal elections to citizens in the country who are 18 years of age and over.
This matter was raised by me-I do not say this was the first time it was raised-during the time the standing committee on privilege and elections was considering amendments and revisions to the Canada Elections Act in 1960. It was in that committee in May 19, 1960, that the proposal I made then, the same one as I am making now, was considered and defeated by a vote of 8 to 2. Subsequent to that, in the same session of 1960, when the bill was reported from the committee, we moved a procedural motion on third reading with the clear intent of providing the right to vote to people of 18 years of age. This amendment did not receive the support of the majority of the members of the house. The Liberals voted with us on that occasion, even though they had voted against us in the committee.
The members on the government side supported the contention advanced by the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) that it was not the appropriate time to extend the franchise to people of 18 years. At that time the Prime Minister made an interesting comment or two which I should like to quote. I find this on page 6279 of Hansard for July 14, 1960:
I think it is one of those things that might very well be studied in detail by a committee at a subsequent session of parliament,-
He also said:
In a subsequent session I will join with hon. members in giving the membership of the house an adequate opportunity to fully explore all the considerations relative to this question:
Now, I quoted those words, Mr. Speaker, in moving the second reading of a bill identical to this which was dealt with at the last session and debate upon which was entered on February 14, 1961. There were five other members representing the other two parties in the house, in addition to myself, who spoke on the bill. None of them objected to extending a franchise to people of the age of 18, although there was some slight disagreement expressed and some reluctance indicated about whether or not 1961 was the appropriate time to proceed with this measure. I do not intend, because I do not believe it really helps, to go into these specific objections which were raised. I feel they are relatively minor compared with the basic principle of the extension of the right to vote to people who are 18 years of age.

Some of the provinces, Mr. Speaker, have a voting age which is less than 21, notably my own province of British Columbia, which some time in 1954, I believe, extended the franchise to those 19 years of age. The adjacent province of Alberta also has a voting age of 19, while Saskatchewan has a voting age of 18. The bill which is before us now seeks to establish a voting age of 18. I suppose as between 18 or 19 one could make an equally effective argument, depending on which age one chose. I am not adamant that it must be 18 years of age, but the basic principle is that it should be lowered to take into account certain factors which exist at the moment and which have been developing in Canada, as in other countries, for some time.
In 1960 during the hearings of the committee on privileges and elections there was placed a tabulation on the record at pages 323 and 324, a tabulation prepared by the chief electoral officer from material contained in the Statesman's Year Book of 1959, indicating the number of countries which have voting ages which are less than 21 years. It also indicates that there are some countries which require that persons be older than 21 years of age before obtaining the right to vote. The tabulation extends from 18 years of age, as is the case in the province of Saskatchewan and the states of Georgia, Kentucky and Alaska, to 25 years of age as required in the Netherlands. However the majority of countries place the age at 21 years.
I do not intend to make specific reference to each country listed in the tabular form. That information is readily available and I am sure the Statesman's Year Book for the years subsequent to 1959 would bring that information up to date.
These are some of the reasons why I think we should extend the franchise to those aged 18 years. First, over the last few years-and this has been greatly intensified since the start of world war II-there has been a great change in the form of communications both within a country and between countries. This has been due to the advent of television and radio, and with the placement in other countries of representatives of news service agencies we find that normally on the day which various political events occur in other countries we know about them here. They come to our attention as adults, and persons who are 18 years of age also know about them.
Then too, during the last few years-and I hope this will continue-there have been more opportunities for people to acquire a higher education. There have been more opportunities to proceed further in school and in formal education than was the case 20 or 30 years ago. Also there is the other factor of

the attraction to individuals to leave school in order to work in industry at fairly decent wages. There is the attraction for them to marry at a younger age and I believe all these factors tend to make our 18 year old people more mature and give them a better understanding of political and sociological matters than was the case a number of years ago.
Sometimes one hears the argument that a person aged 18 years is not mature enough to make a reasonable or mature decision with respect to voting and might be misled by a variety of factors, and thus not be able to make a mature judgment in so far as the party he or she should support is concerned. However, we sometimes find that age and maturity are not necessarily connected. I am sure most of us have run into individuals who are 25, 30, 35 or 40 years of age who have cast doubts on the maturity of individuals in those age groups. It is true, however, that if we talk about young people aged 9, 10 or 11 years then there is some validity to the argument about their ability to express a mature judgment on matters such as this.
That is why I said earlier that I am not particularly tied to the age of 18 but selected it arbitrarily, the same as the age of 21 was selected arbitrarily and is now a sort of arbitrary determination. The impact of greater educational opportunities, the participation by younger people in our economic life, their participation in the married state and in a variety of other things all bring them a better understanding of political and socio-economic matters. Therefore I believe they have a sufficiently sound ability to judge and vote. It would be a correct thing to recognize these factors and to recognize that here is a group of people which, to all intents and purposes in a general way is contributing to a large extent to our economy, to our tax structure, is concerned with activities in the House of Commons and participates in political matters to the extent that it is able to do so. The way to recognize the group is to extend it the right to vote in federal elections when its members reach the age of 18 years.
I believe this bill, if it receives second reading, should be referred to the committee on privileges and elections, as was indicated by the Prime Minister. Of a former occasion he indicated that and said he would support such a motion at a subsequent session. Apparently the last session was not the subsequent session to which he referred. Perhaps this is the one he means, and I would be glad to have it referred to the committee in order that an opportunity might be afforded to people who are interested in this matter to appear before the committee and
Canada Elections Act
express their views so that the committee can evaluate the question itself, can assess the body of public opinion that exists either in favour of or against it, and report the bill back to this house after it has been given careful consideration.
As I said earlier, the house was so agreeable to the bill which preceded this one, extending the franchise to people who heretofore had been denied the right to vote, that I would point out this bill does substantially the same thing except that it is not a geographic extension. It is an age extension and I hope the house will be agreeable to giving the measure its support.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO REDUCE AGE OF VOTERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when we were examining the Canada Elections Act, I supported the resolution introduced by the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard) who, at the time, recommended that the voting age be reduced from 21 to 18.
I could add that the platform of the Liberal party provides for such a reduction in the age of voters.
However, I disagree slightly with the member for Skeena who said a while ago that the age of 21 had been chosen arbitrarily. That is incorrect. At the time, that age was adopted because 21 is the age when a person becomes legally of age and can act on his own and for himself.
The reason we are now recommending that the voting age be reduced to 18 is that young men of that age are liable to be enrolled for the defence of their country.
They risk their lives and yet they have no choice about it. They do not even have a word to say about decisions which could cause them to die prematurely.
Consequently, since they can be enrolled at the age of 18 for the defence of their country, they should have the right to decide on their own what they should do.
Some will say that the voting age for our force members is 18. That is true. Members of the active forces are allowed to vote at 18.
It is precisely because they can be enrolled and because, at present, only their elders can take definite decisions in that connection, that I feel they should have the right to vote. Since they can be the victims of such decisions, they should at least have a part in them.
This does not mean that everything will change.

Canada Elections Act
Some may feel that young people are not mature enough to decide how to vote. I recall what the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillin-gate (Mr. Pickersgill) used to say when the matter was brought up: "At the age of 18, being from a Conservative family, I was a Conservative; upon reaching 21, the age of reason, I became a Liberal".
But that is one case. I know that the majority of young people, today, have had much more schooling than those of 21 and over had 10, 15 or 25 years ago. Today's youth is better informed because of television and newspapers, which fill modern homes. Nowadays, the young people are much better prepared to play their part in the community at 18 than people of my generation were at that age.
Well, for all those reasons, we can support the resolution introduced by the hon. member for Skeena. I think the Liberals will be happy to support this bill and specially to send it to the committee on privileges and elections, so that those who have representations to make can put them before the committee and thus better inform the house.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I spoke on this bill a year ago and I was in favour of reducing the age limit for voting to 18. I believe that when I was 18 years old I was just as good a man as I am now, and I was a good Conservative.
In our country, where they work big machinery, a boy does not wait until he is 21 to run a tractor, a combine, a big disker or anything like that; he is up on them when he is 16 or 17, and when he is 18 he is a mature man. Many a time I have been by fields and seen a boy of 18 driving a big combine. They are raised for that.
We are living in a different world altogether to the world in which we were living when I was a kid. My father probably would not let me go in the barn when I was 18; he was afraid that I was just a big kid and I would get hurt. But now I can go anywhere. In the army I met numerous boys 18 years old and younger, and they certainly should have had the vote. They were just as good when action started as the fellow who was 21, and a lot better than the fellow who was 35 or 40, whose nerves had been hurt by his wife or something like that.
As I say, I am in favour of this age limit being reduced to 18. If young people are not smart then, they never will be smart. We get
[Mr. Caron.)
all kinds. We get many who should not have the vote-we know that-but we cannot make a distinction here or there.
I am going to end my little talk by saying I am in favour of people voting at the age of 18. I think they will do as well, and if a war comes along-and the clouds are loaded with that-a young man of 18 will be one of the first to be called up and he will have to say his piece.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO REDUCE AGE OF VOTERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have given a great deal of thought and consideration to the bill introduced by the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard) and I am inclined to support it. I am going to spell out the reasons why I support it. One cannot help thinking that age 21 is an archaic age limit that was set in times gone by when it was thought that at 21 a person was of mature age and could make decisions. In our law of contract right now a person under 21 years of age can enter into a contract, which he or she can repudiate upon reaching maturity. They are considered minors in the eyes of the law until they are 21 years of age. Unless they are 21 they cannot enter into a contract of sale without there being the risk of their repudiating it upon reaching maturity. However, I believe that the right to vote cannot be put in the same category as the right to enter into a contract.
The age at which the right to vote is given varies in different countries. As the hon. member for Skeena has mentioned, in Holland it is 25 years of age. Apparently the Dutch feel that a person is not mature enough to make political decisions until he is 25 years old. In Denmark it is 23 years of age, in Turkey 22, and in Costa Rica 20, but it is 18 if the person is married or is a school teacher. Apparently in the eyes of those people marriage gives a person a certain maturity.
In many other phases of our life 18 is considered a mature age, and in this connection we cannot help but think of our marriage laws. In most of the provinces-I believe in all the provinces; I know it is the case in Manitoba-a female who is 18 years of age can marry without the consent of her parents. Marriage, apart from the fact that it is given a certain sanctity by the church, is a contract; a young man or woman enters into a contract to love, honour and obey and take the other partner for better or for worse, often for worse. Many marriages of young people have proven very successful; many have been more successful than the marriages of those of a more mature age. The marriage contract is a contract of which society approves. These young people take

on the parental obligations of raising a family and they are considered mature enough to do this. A young man and a young woman are mature enough to renounce their freedom by joining with each other in a partnership and living together.
There is another profession where a person is considered mature at 18. I have in mind the teaching profession. We do not hesitate to engage a teacher, male or female, when he or she has reached the age of 18. We do not hesitate to entrust our children to their care. We trust them not only to educate our children but also to mould their characters. Our departments of education do not hesitate to grant them certificates whereby they are qualified to teach in our schools. The responsibility of a teacher is a great responsibility. If we adhered to the old, archaic idea that no one is mature before the age of 21, we would not trust these young men and women with the care of our children. But there are thousands of these young people teaching in our schools today and doing a mighty wonderful job at that, raising Canadians to become good and loyal citizens. Proper guidance from them supplements the education which the children receive from their parents.
I think of something else. Our young men and women graduate from universities at a considerably younger age nowadays than they did in my time. My daughter graduated when she was 19 and thousands of men and women graduate from universities at that age with honours and degrees. Could they be considered as people whose judgment is so immature that they cannot make up their minds what party to choose or what party to vote for? Are they not mature enough at that age to use correct judgment as to the various platforms or policies submitted by the political parties in this dominion of ours?
One is led to think that we are depriving these people of a right to express themselves by saying that regardless of intelligence and regardless of mental maturity the only yard stick shall 'be the age of 21. One of the speakers who preceded me mentioned military service. I am in complete agreement with what he said. If a young man is old enough to accept command or to give commands, to understand discipline or to understand the cause for which he fights in the defence of this country he is, I believe, mature enough to be granted a vote. I realize that as the law stands those who are serving in the armed forces have the vote. But in time of crisis 18 is the age at which we draft young men into the army. Eighteen is the age at which we accept them as volunteers. The age of 18 is however, according to our present
Canada Elections Act
law, the age at which a young man or woman cannot use good judgment in deciding on the issues of the day.
It is interesting to note that a number of South American countries have a lower voting age. That is not popular in Europe. As I have already said, some European countries such as Holland, hold on to the age of 25 as being the age at which a person can vote. But Bolivia, Venezuela and Mexico all permit people to vote at the age of 18.
Speakers who preceded me have mentioned the fact that there are three provinces in Canada which have lowered the voting age from 21. But taking it all in all there is another argument which I would advance in support of my contention. The young Progressive Conservatives and, I believe, the young Liberal associations have on many occasions considered resolutions to request their parties to lower the voting age. In the limited time I have had at my disposal I have not been able to find any record of resolutions in the past, but I know this is in the minds of these young people, and I think it is nothing but fair.
I know there are others who wish to express their opinions on the subject and therefore I am cutting my remarks short.

speakeroldname: Mr. E. L. Morris (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO REDUCE AGE OF VOTERS
speechtext:
In
the idea of an earlier voting age I can find little flaw. The argument against it seems to follow two lines, first, that 18 year olds are erratic and in secret communion with far leftists or worse, and that though they are able to use logarithms, count down space missiles, have babies, make pills and fly jets they do not have the acumen, the perspective or the judgment to make a choice among political candidates-that is, unless they have already volunteered to be shot at, whereupon we give them the vote.
We allow these young people to go to jail in Canada but not to the polling booths. They cannot, it is said, make legal contracts but has anyone heard of the Department of National Revenue turning away an income tax return because it is signed by an 18 year old? In one democratic domain where the fires of freedom seem to us to burn as fiercely and gleam as brightly as they ever did, men heaved tea chests into the sea six long generations ago precisely in defence of this principle. "No taxation without representation", they said, and away went the tea chests.
It is said that Canada's 526,000 young men between the ages of 18 and 21 and her 511,000 young women between the ages of 18 and 21 are radical. Good. Anyone who means to make anything of life ought to be radical at some time. What finer, gayer, more wonderful time

Canada Elections Act
is there to be radical than when you are young? I believe that 99.9 per cent of the world's advancement has been brought about by people who would not conform because they could not conform.
What is a radical? Most people some of the time and some people all of the time define a radical as a man or woman who does not agree with them. Suppose we use softening words, that instead of radicalism we speak of youth's erraticism, instability, wobbling, immaturity? Who can say that immaturity automatically ceases and maturity begins on one's twenty first birthday?
In between the nuclear tests what are the marks of 1962's adolescents? No trimming and no trembling; devoid of timidity and baseness; tremendous when they are right and even more tremendous when they are wrong, as they occasionally are, not yet having reached the safety first or guaranteed existence; still free from fear and gain-those old perverters of mankind.
In the United States it is said that every young American is born a Democrat and stays that way until he acquires a mortgage, whereupon he becomes a Republican. Nothing gives a sense of responsibility like being made responsible. Eighteen year olds marry, have babies, pay taxes, go into the army, share in the costs of government, share in the duties of the state, but do not share in the rights so long as they are denied the vote.
Mr. Speaker, the prosecution rests.

Mr. Speaker, it has been my privilege to participate in previous debates on this and similar bills both in the house and in the privileges and elections committee when this question came under scrutiny at the time when that committee reviewed, and in my opinion greatly improved, the Canada Elections Act a few years ago. I am not going to take up much of the time of the house today because there are several other hon. members who wish to record their views and who have been deprived of an opportunity in the past.
It seems to me that the usefulness and value of the discussions during the private members hour has been illustrated in an important way. Following my remarks and submissions in previous debates, my contributions being far less eloquent than those of the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat although generally along the same lines advanced by the hon. member in his arguments today, I received a number of phone calls and letters and had a number of discussions.
Having supported the principle of this bill, as I said, I was confronted by an argument which I found very difficult to refute. If this bill does go to the committee I hope the single

point I am about to raise will come under careful scrutiny. I also hope that hon. gentlemen who follow me in this debate will address themselves to this question.
I have reference to the incidence of automobile accidents and the risk attached to the driver of a car under age 21, and the reflection of that risk among that age group not only in the accident rate but in the insurance rates that are charged. While this does not support the proposition it is a factor in the argument which has to be confronted and answered.
I have not had sufficient time to pursue this matter as I would like to, but I am given to understand that the number of accidents and the corresponding insurance rate is much higher at the age which the hon. gentleman who is sponsoring this bill proposes to establish as the voting age.
I am reluctant to go beyond that. I will only repeat that this argument has been raised and I have not really been able to effectively refute it. I feel that consideration should be given to it in any future action taken along these lines.

speakeroldname: Mr. M. J. A. Lambert (Edmonton West):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Revenue
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO REDUCE AGE OF VOTERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to speak on the bill this afternoon I realize, as one who is over age 21, that we who are addressing ourselves to this question do not wish to give the impression that we are speaking of the "haves" as opposed to the "have nots". I must say that when I was considerably younger I would have viewed this bill with a great deal more enthusiasm than I do today.
In the last 25 years or so we have seen agitation for this change in the voting age. Some of the provinces-and only the provinces-have acceded to the request to make changes allowing people under age 21 to vote. It might be instructive to inquire into the motives of those provincial administrations that have made this change. I think we should get to the bottom of this. One of the points we must consider in determining whether a person should have a right to vote is that this is a right, a privilege. I think all hon. members will agree that a right implies a responsibility. There is no such thing as a right without a corresponding duty or responsibility. If there is a right to vote there must be the responsibility of the exercise of that right.
In certain parts of Canada in certain types of elections there is a notorious degree of disinterest on the part of the electorate. The voting age in the province of Alberta has been lowered to 19. It would be most illuminating to know just what proportion of the age group between 19 and 20 exercised in the provincial elections the right that was

given them as a great boon and bounty. I would put it to hon. members of this house, that from my observation they were somewhat less active in exercising their right than were those of a more mature age. We also know that in municipalities voting is still limited to those 21 and over. I stand to be corrected if necessary in what I am about to say. I do not know whether a property owner under the age of 21 would have the right to vote as a burgess, but I would be of the opinion that the overriding qualification of the age of 21 would apply.
The hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard) made one point with which I agree fully, that age does not equal maturity. Certainly we will agree with that because we know there are some people who at the age of 16 are quite as mature in their approach to affairs of a public nature as their neighbours who may be double that age. There is an old adage that there is no fool quite like an old fool. Yet one must arrive at a dividing line somewhere. What is it going to be? Is it to be the yardstick of age?
I will be the first to admit that this yardstick may not be the most perfect, but before we seek to make a change I suggest that we must find a better yardstick and at the same time one that must be practical. It might be suggested that an intelligence test might be a better yardstick for voting qualification or possibly a test as to awareness of public affairs. But just how would you administer such a test so as to qualify people?
I thought the hon. member for Hull (Mr. Caron) developed an argument which I cannot let pass. He stated that because young men and women may be inducted into the armed services at the age of 18 they should have the right to decide whether they should be brought into the armed services. We know that once they have entered military service they are entitled to vote, but I submit that this is a concession to or derogation from the yardstick of age that we have adopted in view of the fact of military service. It is not a concession to the reasoning that the median age should be 21.
To get back to the argument of the hon. member for Hull, I think we could say quite easily that as parents we make very serious decisions which affect our teenage children. Sometimes they object; but is it ever suggested by anyone of serious mind that such decisions within the family should be based on a majority vote, including the vote of teenagers? I think we would have a rather difficult time. I know some of them might like it but we do not accept it as a normal course of conduct.
I think we have to come back to the overriding principle that within practical limits
Canada Elections Act
we are trying to determine what shall be the median age. As I indicated before, this may not be the most perfect way, but I submit to hon. members that in advocating a change it must be a change for the better, and I wonder whether one can say that a change in the voting age would bring a greater awareness of public affairs and that as a result we would get better administration. I seriously question that.
There was something said about young people today being much more aware of public affairs than young people were a generation ago. I submit that is entirely a matter of opinion. I have attended many functions in some of our schools. I have heard young people talk on matters of everyday life and I do not think this generation is any better in that regard than its predecessor or those who went before. They are still interested in those things which, frankly, do not come within the scope of public affairs on which they would vote.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, I adopt the attitude that we must have a yardstick. In the light of experience the yardstick of 21 years of age has proved to be reasonably good. It certainly ties with the legal concept of majority, and unless one can find cogent reasons that will give us definite advantages I do not believe we should change the voting age. I am sorry, but at the moment I do not think I can support the bill.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, no one is more conscious of the fact than I am that in speaking against the bill I am laying myself open to the certain criticism that, as an old man, I want to maintain the status quo. Those of advanced years are always open to that accusation and I face it in advance.
I should like to use the words that were used by the hon. member who just took his seat because he expressed what is in my mind. The mover of the bill referred to the age of 21 as arbitrary. I was on the point of asking him if he thought that was an entirely fair statement having regard to the fact that it is presumably in line with the age of 21 being the age of legal liability and to that extent it is not wholly arbitrary. It is a basis and, as the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) said, there should be cogent reasons for changing it. As it has been accepted for years and we have got used to this state of affairs, I think it is reasonable that we should ask that there should be cogent reasons for making a change.
The only member who seemed to me to come anywhere near giving cogent reasons was the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Morris). He had a very tidy, neat and well worked out

Business of the House argument that dovetailed quite well but I rather thought that in his final words his argument had an American flavour. The thing that is difficult to face is the fact that we do take men in the army at 18 but to some extent at any rate their case is covered by legislation. While there is no one who has better reason to know what those between the ages of 18 and 21 can do in wartime, nevertheless it seems to me that the tests which should apply are quite different. Gallant fellows from 18 to 21 do things that nobody else could do and do them partly because they do not bother with questions of judgment. They do not look before and after. They have a headlong attitude toward life which has been very valuable to this country but which would perhaps not contribute to the exercise of balanced judgment.
